items.q: introduced herself and me to Turk. And we became really quite friendly with the band, particularly with Turk

ctx.x: Yeah. Well, it's nice to have confirmation. Instead of something, say, coming from my faith all along. And also I found a napkin signed by some people from the Italian Village at 115 Columbus Avenue, San Francisco.

Oh, yeah, that was, the Italian Village was a nightclub down more or less near the North Beach area in San Francisco. And for some years, the Turk Murphy Band worked in the, I think, least and worked in the lower level of the place. They had a, you know, standard nightclub and show and restaurant up above. And the, the Murphy Band worked below. And this was at least from 1952, and I suspect a little bit earlier, until they got into the earthquake lagoon business a number of years later. When I was an intern in…

items.title: Bernard Steinau Interview, 1978-08-01
items.q: they had, as I remember, uh, two trumpets and a Turk Murphy on trombone

ctx.x: But, uh, it depended a lot. For example, I very much liked some of the so-called jazz revival white bands. And I, in fact, the first band that ever, that I ever listened to, uh, in person. And that really excited me was Lou Waters' jazz band. Well, the Yerba Buena Jazz Band, which I caught in San Francisco in, I think, late November of 1945. No, no, it was late November of 1946, at the, uh, Dawn Club off of Market, about a block. And, uh, I was on my way back home to New Orleans after having been processed out of…

Were there many people who liked to go listen to black bands and collect the different things? Collected their records, uh? Not, not in New Orleans. I don't know that there ever have been in New Orleans. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We were, around the New Orleans Record Shop, we'd see the people. Certainly. Who'd come in and buy the records. And I'm, I'm trying to think of who I saw that came in there.
